overview: Magnus Eriksson was king of Sweden and Norway whose long reign linked the two kingdoms before political opposition displaced him. The profile is anchored by concrete turning points: 1319 — Becomes king of Sweden and Norway; 1332 — Acquires Scania; 1364 — Deposed in Sweden.
He died in 1374, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Magnus Eriksson was king of Sweden and Norway whose long reign linked the two kingdoms before political opposition displaced him. The profile is anchored by concrete turning points: 1319 — Becomes king of Sweden and Norway; 1332 — Acquires Scania; 1364 — Deposed in Sweden.
He died in 1374, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Magnus Eriksson was born c. 1316. His family background is usually placed in House of Bjälbo, though early Scandinavian genealogy can be uncertain and politically shaped.
Magnus Eriksson's early life belonged to the medieval Scandinavian world, where kinship, sea routes, church contacts, assemblies, and armed followings shaped the opportunities available to a ruler.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Magnus Eriksson ruled both Sweden and Norway as a child-king and is remembered as a well-meaning but ultimately unsuccessful monarch whose long reign ended in deposition and disaster. The sources present a ruler associated with significant achievements — a national law code for Sweden, the abolition of thralldom — yet dogged by financial difficulty, noble revolt, and the catastrophe of the Black Death that struck during his reign.

His reputation suffered greatly from a hostile tradition: the prophecies attributed to Saint Birgitta of Sweden condemned him sharply, and rumours about his personal conduct circulated among his enemies. This propaganda, much of it driven by aristocratic and religious opponents, shaped a harshly negative memory that modern historians treat with caution.

What the record more securely supports is a ruler of reforming intentions overwhelmed by rebellion, plague, debt, and dynastic rivalry, who lost first Sweden and then his footing in Norway and drowned in exile. He is remembered as a tragic and much-maligned king, his real character partly buried beneath the condemnation of his enemies.

contentSections.title: As king of Sweden and Norway
paragraphs: Magnus Eriksson inherited both Sweden and Norway as a child. His long reign involved law, aristocratic politics, plague-era pressures, and conflict with his son and rivals.
As King of Sweden, King of Norway, Magnus Eriksson had to turn dynastic claim into workable authority through alliances, military pressure, church support, and acceptance by regional elites.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Died in 1374, traditionally by drowning off Bømlo in Norway, after losing effective power in both Sweden and Norway.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: He is remembered as a shared Scandinavian ruler and a key figure before the Kalmar Union era.
Later saga, saintly, or national traditions often amplified Magnus Eriksson's reputation, so the article separates near-contemporary evidence from later memory where possible.

timeline.title: Acquires Scania
timeline.description: Magnus acquired Scania from Denmark, briefly expanding Swedish royal power in the southern Baltic region.

timeline.title: Deposed in Sweden
timeline.description: Swedish opposition brought Albert of Mecklenburg to power in 1364, ending Magnus’s effective rule in Sweden.
